means:
Serving as a **temporary substitute**, thrown together from whatever happened to be lying around: *a makeshift raft*, *a makeshift office at the kitchen table*.

*Temporary* says only "not for long." **Makeshift** adds two things: it was **improvised**, and it is **slightly inadequate** — it does the job, but visibly badly. There's a double edge to it. Calling a solution makeshift half-praises the resourcefulness and half-admits the thing is crude and will have to be replaced.
trick_line: Nothing **makeshift** stays put — the second half of the word is **shift**.
trick_unpack: A makeshift thing is built to be shifted out the moment the real one arrives.
sentences: Cut off by the flood, the villagers erected a **makeshift** bridge of scaffolding planks and rope.
We had no music stand, so he propped the sheet on a **makeshift** one made of two textbooks and a shoebox.
in_the_wild: News reports run on this word: a **makeshift memorial** of flowers and candles on a pavement, **makeshift hospitals** in convention centres during Covid. Both are the same idea — real need, no proper facility, so people build one out of what's to hand.
etymology:
From the old phrase **"to make shift"** = *to contrive, to manage somehow*. **Shift** here means **an expedient**, not movement.

That older sense unlocks a cousin: **shiftless** = not lazy in the sleepy sense but **lacking resourcefulness**, unable to contrive anything for yourself.
one_line: A crude temporary substitute made from whatever's at hand.
root: shift (Old English sciftan — to arrange, contrive; hence "an expedient")
